CONSTITUTION, BY-LAWS, AND UNIVERSITY MANUAL COMMITTEE Report #2023-2024-08 - Proposed changes to Chapter 8 Academic Regulations FACULTY SENATE - December 7, 2023 Context: Revised language that provides students called to military service options for missed course work.
Federal regulations have specific stipulations about the use of “Incomplete” as a grade option that conflict with existing University Manual language.
This companion change to Report #2023-2024-07 provides clarification for this conflict.
Existing language: 8.53.20 Incomplete.
A student shall receive a temporary grade of “Incomplete” when course work has been passing but is not completed by the end of the semester due to documented extenuating circumstances beyond the ability of the student to predict and control, such as a serious illness or medical condition, or another compelling reason which justifies the grade.
An instructor who issues a grade of “Incomplete” may forward a written explanation to the student’s academic dean.

Assignment of the temporary grade of Incomplete is made sparingly and presumes both that the student intends and will be able to complete the coursework in the established time frame, and that the instructor intends and will be able to review the completed work in that established time frame. #15-16-30 #22-23-30 Proposed language: 8.53.20 Incomplete.

V. 23.09.29 CURRICULUM & STANDARDS COMMITTEE FACULTY SENATE OFFICE URI Curriculum & Standards Committee Non-Standard form for curricular changes Only to be used in cases not appropriate for Kuali A Proposal to Fully Integrate the Public Relations Program into the Department of Journalism, Creating a New Department of Journalism and Public Relations Date: 10/27/23 Proposer Name: Professor Norbert Mundorf Department: Communication Studies 1.
Describe the change you are proposing.
This organization change will bring the Public Relations B.A. program, which is currently housed in the Communication Studies department, and the Journalism B.A. program together in a new Journalism and Public Relations department. 2.
Give the rationale for your proposed change.
In 1997, the B.A. in Public Relations was approved as an interdepartmental program jointly run by the Communication Studies department and the Journalism department.

The original legislation (Bill #96- 97-26) called for the program to be administered on a “three-year rotating basis by the Chairs of Journalism and Communication Studies” with an “advisory/admissions committee” comprised of both chairs from the respective departments and the faculty who taught in the program.
Somewhere in the twenty-five plus years that have elapsed since the original proposal, the Public Relations program was effectively subsumed by Communication Studies and the interdepartmental structure of the original vision was lost.
During the academic program review of Journalism this past year, external reviewers suggested the Journalism curriculum would benefit from a “rethinking of [Harrington’s] overall department structure.” While it was originally proposed that the department might merge with the program in Sports Media Communication, subsequent conversations with faculty suggested that public relations would be a better fit as this pairing is common in institutions across the country and presents additional opportunities for collaboration due to the curricular overlap between the two programs.

Interestingly, the original proposal to create the public relations program also emphasized the importance of this relationship: “Because the existing Public Relations courses are Journalism courses, CASC Report 2023-2024-04B Page 2 of 7

V. 23.09.29 because the existing minor has been administered by the chair of Journalism, and because of the extent of the chair’s involvement in the existing internship program, the chair of Journalism will serve as the initial administrator of the program.” Following the guidance of the reviewers and in the spirit of the original vision for this program, the proposed organizational change will restore the interdisciplinary vision for the Public Relations program. It will allow for resource sharing and interdisciplinary collaboration between programs and will also help to rectify a primary issue addressed in the Journalism academic program review, namely, the absence of a Chair. In order to address this leadership gap and ensure a successful start to this new department, a search for a Full Professor who will Chair this new department is currently underway. 3. This change will affect the Public Relations BA program (currently housed in Communication Studies department) and Journalism BA program and Journalism department. These units are housed in the Harrington School of Communication and Media in the College of Arts and Sciences. 4. Include any necessary letters of support. Letters of support are included from the faculty of the public relations program , the department of Journalism, the Director of the Harrington School of Communication and Media, and the Dean of Arts and Sciences. 29 October 2023 Support for new Department of Journalism and Public Relations As Dean of Arts and Sciences, I fully support the proposed integration of Public Relations with the Journalism Department to create a new Department of Journalism and Public Relations. This merger does not impact the academic programs in any way. Nationally, many institutions have journalism and public relations programs in the same department. Students and faculty both benefit from the synergies between the two disciplines. The merger will also enable more effective use of resources, while also freeing the Department of Communication Studies to focus more fully on their major, as well as continue to provide a home for the rapidly expanding sports communication and media major. The Journalism and Public Relations faculty have all discussed and confirmed their agreement to merge. A full professor line has been allocated for this initiative, and the individual hired will serve as chair; a search committee composed of faculty from both majors has been established. Further, I am committed to providing faculty lines to move fully resource both majors given their import and student interest. This is an exciting move for both programs and for the Harrington School, and I fully support the transition. Jeannette E. Riley Dean, Arts and Sciences CASC Report 2023-2024-04B Page 4 of 7

CASC Procedures

The Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) Procedures CASC examines course and program proposals to ensure they are comprehensible and user-friendly for undergraduate students.
Within the Kuali proposal, we examine all ﬁelds to conﬁrm clear details vital to student success, such as prerequisites, course rationale and description, the number of seats and sections offered per year, and syllabi.
Syllabi should accompany all major course proposals (new classes, signiﬁcant modiﬁcations to a course).
To ensure proposal syllabi will be clear to students, we look for: ● straight-forward course information (class description & objectives, method of instruction); ● clear course policies, structures, and methods of teaching; ● clarity regarding grade scale & methods, assignments, and how coursework connects to credit hours; ● current information about accessible technological resources and apps necessary for the class; Further, students are best served by having up-to-date information on support services such as DAI; illness policies; and procedures reﬂecting current University standards.
Where these items are overlooked or out-of-date, CASC may provide friendly feedback.

Also, ATL has resources and templates for syllabi ( https://web.uri.edu/atl/design/syllabus/ ).
New courses should provide supporting documentation uploaded by the chair of the department/academic unit into the proper Kuali ﬁeld, indicating the date that their department/program voted to approve the course.
Program-level proposals should include all materials relevant to the new program/proposed changes, including supporting documentation from other academic units impacted by these changes.
All program and applicable accreditation requirements should be listed .
The Kuali ﬁelds for program proposals should include courses impacted by changes.
Course and Program Overlap Overlap is when a newly proposed or modiﬁed course/program intersects with the content of an existing course or program.
The amount of overlap might range from small (the topics of a single class) to approaching virtual duplication.
Proposers and curriculum approval committees can use search features within Kuali to compare other current and proposed courses/programs for potential overlap.

When CASC recognizes potential overlap, they will ask the course proposer and department/instructor to consult regarding the degree and signiﬁcance of overlap.
Even with substantial replication in content, there might be key differences in approach.
As CASC cannot be experts in all disciplines, we request that the proposer and faculty for the existing course/program work together.
This collaboration can be documented in a statement communicating the resolution to CASC.
If this collaboration cannot occur, CASC exercises its best judgment regarding student beneﬁt.
Note: overlap issues can also be addressed on the Faculty Senate ﬂoor or even at ﬁnal approval with the President.
We also encourage colleges to check for overlap themselves.
Starting in Fall 2025, CASC’s ‘Proposed Temporary and Permanent Courses/Programs’ email will be distributed at the end of the last full week of each month.
We encourage each college’s curriculum committee to meet during the ﬁrst full week of each month and, as part of their deliberations, carefully consider all newly proposed offerings in that CASC newsletter for potential overlap.

Any overlapping courses/programs should be reported to Genviéve Spitale ( genvieve.spitale@uri.edu ); the course/program will not be reviewed until the originating and overlapping colleges agree in writing that either the original proposal or a revised version can move forward for CASC/Gen Ed/Grad Council consideration.

NEW CERTIFICATES, MINORS, or SPECIALIZATIONS COLLEGE OF EDUCATION: Minor in Global Education Studies, see Appendix H Global Education Studies (GES) minor allows students to explore globalization and internationalization of education and educational policies using the critical lens of equity and social justice, human rights and global citizenship.
The minor will prepare students with a diversity of backgrounds with the skill sets to become change agents and leaders in education in today’s globalized world.
This minor is part of the College of Education, as K-16 education are important components of the program.
However, students from all majors are welcome to participate or take courses in the minor.
Students interested in pursuing careers in and outside of the U.S. in the field of K-16 education, governmental and non-governmental organizations, international agencies, further their studies of international issues are especially encouraged to pursue this minor.
The curriculum is focused on expanding students’ knowledge, skills, and understanding of specific comparative and international theories, concepts, and practices in education.

The minor includes a requirement for participation in a faculty-led program in one of the College of Education’s study abroad programs in education or equivalent international experience such as COIL.
To declare a minor in Global Studies in Education a student must contact their major academic advisor at their College.
A program advisor at the College of Education will facilitate the students’ progress toward the minor and help assure that all requirements will be met for completion of the minor.
Minor Requirements: Global Education Studies (GES) minors must complete 18 or more credits related to global, comparative, and international education offered by different departments.
Requirements include a core of nine credits at the College of Education as follows: 1) EDC441-Comparative and International Education; 2) EDC330-Introduction to MLL Education; 3) Participation in a Faculty led study abroad program or an internship that is equivalent (i.e.
COIL (Collaborative Online International Learning, transfer course from another study abroad program).
We have a partnership with BridgeTEFL, students can transfer credits from this program, toward certification to teach English abroad.

Students will also choose a minimum of one language course from the Languages department or proficiency in another language that may not be offered in the languages department.
This can be waived for a student who has grown up in a multilingual household, or who has lived and studied at least three years or more in a foreign country including grades 1-12 (or equivalent).
For those students, these three credits can be replaced with electives.
Finally, students will take two electives from the approved courses.
Non-Education majors must also take EDC103 G in place of one of their electives.
Other international/global courses may be used as electives if approved by advisor.

Students who complete the program understand how to critically and effectively evaluate, analyze, and produce sports media and communication products using a variety of technologies and media, from their voice for broadcasting to social media platforms for advertising.
